Dialect

/DY-uh-lekt/ - the stress falls on DY · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Dialect means a regional variety of a language.

Two valleys apart, the shepherds speak the same language in different clothes: each village's dialect has its own words for snow and its own way of ending a question.

Worked Example

The soup was 'potlikker' at the southern grandmother's table and 'broth' at the northern one, and the cousins needed a whole summer to stop laughing at each other's verbs. Neither family spoke wrongly; each spoke its region's dialect, a full local system of words, sounds and grammar.

Dialect is bigger than accent and smaller than language: an accent changes only how words sound, while a dialect carries its own vocabulary and grammar — yet its speakers and their neighbors can still mostly understand one another.

How Dialect Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

patois

patois: a regional dialect, especially a homespun, unwritten one

lingo

lingo: informal word for any group's special talk — a trade or hobby can have a lingo, no region required

Antonyms

officialese

officialese: the colorless formal language of documents, belonging to no region at all

mainstream

mainstream: the region-neutral current of a language that broadcasters and textbooks favor

How Strong Is It? — accent → dialect → language

accent vs. dialect

accent vs. dialect: An accent stops short of a dialect: it changes only the sound of words, never the words or the grammar themselves.

language vs. dialect

language vs. dialect: A language goes further than an accent ever does — by that point the divergence is so complete that neighbors need study to understand each other, which is more separation than any dialect creates.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of dialect.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dia

Prefix — dia: across, between (Greek)

Root — lect

Root — lect: speaking; choosing words (Greek legein, to speak)

Put it together

Put it together: Greek dia- means 'across' or 'between,' and legein meant 'to speak': a dialektos was the way talk passes between the people of one place. English kept the sense — a dialect is how a particular region speaks among itself.

Use the root in a new word: lecture

Use the root in a new word: lecture: Tuesday's lecture on glaciers filled the hall, and the speaker never once glanced at her notes.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / linguistic

Use dialect for a region's full variety of a language — words, grammar and sound together. If only the pronunciation differs, say accent; for the everyday speech of ordinary people as opposed to formal language, English has vernacular, a word covered in this unit's reference list. Slang and lingo belong to groups, not regions.
